go mod: 'ambiguous import: found package in multiple modules' after tagging v2
content: I maintain a library and tagged `v2.0.0` on it. Consumers that upgrade now fail at `go build` with `ambiguous import: found package example.com/lib/store in multiple modules: example.com/lib v1.8.3 and example.com/lib/v2 v2.0.0`. The consumer's `go.mod` requires both because a transitive dependency still pins the v1 line. Running `go mod tidy` does not remove either requirement, and `go mod why example.com/lib` points at that transitive dependency. I did add `/v2` to the module path in my own `go.mod` before tagging, and the tag is `v2.0.0` on a repo with no `v2/` subdirectory. Is having both major versions in one build graph supposed to be legal, and if so why is the import ambiguous rather than resolved by the module path?

title: E0502: cannot borrow `map` as mutable while iterating over it in a for loop
future cannot be sent between threads safely because a MutexGuard is held across an await
E0515: cannot return value referencing local variable when returning a &str from a String
content:
I want a helper that formats an id into a label without the caller having to own a `String`. Rust 1.83.

```
fn label(id: u32) -> &'static str {
    let s = format!("item-{id}");
    &s
}
```

```bash
error[E0515]: cannot return reference to local variable `s`
 --> src/lib.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     &s
  |     ^^ returns a reference to data owned by the current function
```

Dropping `'static` gives `error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier` instead, and adding `fn label<'a>(id: u32) -> &'a str` fails the same way. I get that `s` dies at the end of the function, but is there any signature that lets the caller get a `&str` here, or do I have to return `String` and make every call site allocate?

title: cargo build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu fails with 'linker `cc` not found'
content: I am cross-compiling a pure-Rust binary from an x86_64 Ubuntu 24.04 box to aarch64, Rust 1.83. I ran `rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, which succeeded, and `rustup show` lists the target as installed. `cargo build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` still fails at the link step with `error: linker "cc" not found` — and when I point `CC` at `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` the failure changes to a pile of `unrecognized emulation mode` errors from `ld`. The crate has no C dependencies and builds fine for the host target. What exactly does rustup's target component install (and what does it not), and where does the linker for the target get configured — `.cargo/config.toml` or an env var?

title: multiprocessing.Pool hangs on exit when a worker raises a custom exception
asyncio.run() raises 'cannot be called from a running event loop' inside my library helper
content:
I have a sync convenience wrapper around an async client so that scripts can call it without knowing about asyncio. Python 3.13.

```python
import asyncio

async def _fetch(url):
    ...

def fetch(url):
    return asyncio.run(_fetch(url))

async def handler(url):
    return fetch(url)
```

Calling `fetch()` from a plain script works. Calling `handler()` from inside an already running loop blows up with `RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop`. I tried `asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(...)` and got the same class of error plus a DeprecationWarning. Is there a supported way to run a coroutine to completion from sync code that is itself called from a coroutine, or do I have to expose both a sync and an async API?

title: TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes after switching to zoneinfo
content:
I moved a scheduler from `pytz` to `zoneinfo` on Python 3.13 and the duration calculation broke.

```python
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

start = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Europe/Warsaw"))
deadline = datetime.strptime("2026-03-29 03:30", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")
print(deadline - start)
```

```bash
TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
```

Attaching the zone with `deadline.replace(tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Europe/Warsaw"))` makes the error go away, but 2026-03-29 02:30 local is the DST spring-forward gap in that zone and the resulting UTC offset looks wrong to me. What is the correct way to attach a zone to a parsed wall-clock time, and what does `zoneinfo` do for a time that does not exist?

title: pip install fails with ResolutionImpossible between two packages pinning different urllib3
content: On Python 3.13 in a fresh venv, `pip install -r requirements.txt` ends with `ERROR: ResolutionImpossible` and a conflict report saying one package requires `urllib3<2`, another requires `urllib3>=2.0`, and my own file pins `urllib3==2.2.3`. Neither dependency has a release that agrees with the other on PyPI as far as I can tell from their metadata. Backtracking runs for several minutes downloading dozens of old sdists before giving up. I do not want to use `--no-deps` because that just moves the failure to import time. Is there a way to get pip to tell me the minimal set of conflicting requirements rather than the full backtracking log, and is pinning a transitive dependency in the requirements file the right lever here at all?

title: UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x92 reading a CSV exported from Excel
content:
Python 3.13 on macOS, reading a file a colleague exported from Excel on Windows.

```python
import csv

with open("export.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row)
```

```bash
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x92 in position 4117:
invalid start byte
```

`file export.csv` reports `ISO-8859 text, with CRLF line terminators`. Opening with `encoding="latin-1"` reads without an exception but turns the offending characters into a control character rather than the apostrophe I see in Excel. `encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"` gives me question marks. Which encoding actually produces 0x92 for a curly apostrophe, and is there a way to detect this rather than guessing per file?

title: forEach with an async callback returns before the inserts finish in Node 22
ERR_REQUIRE_ESM when requiring node-fetch v3 from a CommonJS file on Node 22
content:
Node 22.11, project has no `"type"` field in package.json, so my files are CommonJS.

```javascript
// scripts/sync.cjs
const fetch = require("node-fetch"); // node-fetch 3.3.2
```

```bash
Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module
/app/node_modules/node-fetch/src/index.js from /app/scripts/sync.cjs not supported.
Instead change the require of index.js to a dynamic import() which is available
in all CommonJS modules.
```

I tried `const { default: fetch } = await import("node-fetch")` but top-level await is not allowed in CJS. Downgrading to node-fetch 2 works. Node 22 has a global `fetch` — is that a full replacement for the cases node-fetch covers (proxy agent, streaming bodies), and if I do need the package, what is the least invasive way to consume an ESM-only dependency from a CJS entry point?

title: MaxListenersExceededWarning: 11 shutdown listeners added after a few thousand requests

ConcurrentModificationException when removing from an ArrayList inside an enhanced for loop
NoSuchMethodError for Preconditions.checkArgument at runtime only, compiles fine
content: Java 21, Maven build. The project compiles cleanly and unit tests pass, but on the server it dies with `java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'void com.google.common.base.Preconditions.checkArgument(boolean, java.lang.String, java.lang.Object)'`. `mvn dependency:tree` shows Guava pulled in twice at different versions through two different libraries, and Maven's nearest-wins resolution picks the older one, while I compile against the newer API that a direct dependency exposes transitively. Adding an explicit direct dependency on the newer Guava fixes it locally, but I want to understand whether that is a real fix or a coincidence of ordering, and whether `dependencyManagement`, a `<exclusions>` block, or the shade plugin's relocation is the right tool when two libraries genuinely need different versions.

AddressSanitizer heap-use-after-free after realloc grows my array
content:
C11, Clang 18, built with `-fsanitize=address`. I keep a second pointer into the buffer for convenience and it goes stale.

```
int *a = malloc(4 * sizeof *a);
int *cursor = a;

a = realloc(a, 1024 * sizeof *a);
cursor[0] = 1;
```

```bash
==7==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x602000000010
WRITE of size 4 at 0x602000000010 thread T0
0x602000000010 is located 0 bytes inside of 16-byte region
freed by thread T0 here:
    #1 in realloc
```

Without the sanitizer the write usually lands somewhere harmless and the bug shows up much later as corrupted data. I also noticed that assigning the result straight back to `a` leaks the original block if `realloc` returns NULL. What is the correct idiom — store offsets instead of pointers, and use a temporary for the `realloc` result?

title: fread into a struct reads shifted values because sizeof is 12 while records are 7 bytes
Composer: class not found after moving it to a new namespace, dump-autoload does not help
content: PHP 8.3, Composer 2.8. I moved `App\Service\Mailer` to `App\Mail\Mailer` and moved the file from `src/Service/Mailer.php` to `src/Mail/Mailer.php`. Every request now dies with `Error: Class "App\Mail\Mailer" not found`. My autoload block maps `"App\\": "src/"` under `psr-4`. I ran `composer dump-autoload -o`, deleted `vendor/composer/autoload_*`, and cleared the framework cache; the generated `autoload_classmap.php` still lists the old FQCN pointing at the old path, which no longer exists. The class name inside the file, the namespace declaration and the directory all match as far as I can see, and the deploy target is Linux while I develop on macOS. What does the optimized classmap key off, and could the case-insensitive filesystem be why this only breaks in production?

title: json_encode() returns false with JSON_ERROR_UTF8 for rows read from a latin1 MySQL table
content:
PHP 8.3 with PDO against MySQL 8. Some rows serialize fine, some make the whole response empty.

```
$rows = $pdo->query('SELECT id, name FROM users')->fetchAll(PDO::FETCH_ASSOC);
$json = json_encode($rows);

var_dump($json);                 // bool(false)
echo json_last_error_msg();      // Malformed UTF-8 characters, possibly incorrectly encoded
```

The table columns are `latin1_swedish_ci` and the connection charset is `utf8mb4`, so I suspect the driver is handing me bytes that are not valid UTF-8. `JSON_INVALID_UTF8_SUBSTITUTE` makes `json_encode` succeed but replaces the accented characters with U+FFFD, which is not acceptable for names. Is `mb_convert_encoding($v, 'UTF-8', 'ISO-8859-1')` on every string field the right repair, or should this be fixed at the connection/collation level so PHP never sees latin1 bytes?

title: PDO throws a syntax error near '10' when binding LIMIT with a bound parameter
content:
PHP 8.3, MySQL 8, PDO with default settings.

```
$limit = $_GET['limit'];               // "10"
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT id FROM posts ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT :limit');
$stmt->bindValue(':limit', $limit, PDO::PARAM_INT);
$stmt->execute();
```

```bash
SQLSTATE[42000]: Syntax error or access violation: 1064 You have an error in your
SQL syntax; check the manual ... near ''10'' at line 1
```

The quotes around 10 in the message tell me the value is going in as a string despite `PDO::PARAM_INT`. Interpolating `(int) $limit` straight into the SQL works but I would rather not build SQL by hand. I have seen `PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => false` suggested — does that change how PARAM_INT is sent, and are there downsides for the rest of my queries if I turn emulation off globally?

title: Hash.new([]) makes every key share one array and nothing is ever stored in the hash
content:
Ruby 3.4. I am grouping records by key and the result is empty even though the array clearly grows.

```
counts = Hash.new([])
counts[:a] << 1
counts[:b] << 2

p counts        # {}
p counts[:a]    # [1, 2]
p counts[:zzz]  # [1, 2]
```

I expected `{a: [1], b: [2]}`. Instead the hash has no keys at all, and every lookup — including keys I never touched — returns the same array holding both values. `Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] }` gives me what I wanted. I would like to understand exactly what the non-block form of `Hash.new` stores and why `<<` on the default never creates a key, since `counts[:a] += [1]` does create one.

title: Bundler: 'Your bundle is locked to nokogiri 1.16.0 but that version could not be found'
content: Ruby 3.4, Bundler 2.5, deploying to a Linux container while developing on an Apple Silicon Mac. `bundle install --deployment` in CI fails with `Your bundle is locked to nokogiri (1.16.0) from rubygems repository https://rubygems.org/, but that version could not be found in that source`. The version does exist on rubygems.org. `Gemfile.lock` has a PLATFORMS section listing only `arm64-darwin-23`, and nokogiri ships precompiled native gems per platform. Running `bundle lock --add-platform x86_64-linux` and committing the lock makes CI pass, but I want to know whether that is the intended workflow or a workaround, and what `bundle install` does differently in deployment mode that makes it refuse to resolve instead of just fetching the gem it needs.

title: Timeout.timeout does not interrupt a catastrophic regexp backtrack in Ruby 3.4
content:
Ruby 3.4. I wrapped user-supplied input matching in `Timeout.timeout` expecting a hard ceiling on the work.

```
require 'timeout'

re = /\A(a+)+\z/
s  = 'a' * 30 + 'b'

Timeout.timeout(1) { re.match?(s) }
```

I expected `Timeout::Error` after one second. Instead the process pins a core for minutes and the block never returns; Ctrl-C does not interrupt it either. If I replace the regexp with `sleep 30`, the timeout fires as documented. So `Timeout` clearly works for some blocking operations and not this one. Is the timeout thread's `raise` only delivered at interrupt check points that the regexp engine never reaches, and is `Regexp.timeout=` the only real defence here?

title: View model never deinits: retain cycle from a closure capturing self in a Combine sink
Swift 6 strict concurrency: capture of non-Sendable self in a @Sendable closure
JSONDecoder .iso8601 throws dataCorrupted on timestamps with fractional seconds
content:
Swift 5.10 on iOS 17, decoding a payload from our own backend.

```
struct Post: Decodable {
    let id: Int
    let createdAt: Date
}

let decoder = JSONDecoder()
decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase
decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601
// payload: {"id": 1, "created_at": "2026-03-11T09:41:12.482Z"}
```

```bash
Swift.DecodingError.dataCorrupted(Swift.DecodingError.Context(
  codingPath: [CodingKeys(stringValue: "createdAt")],
  debugDescription: "Expected date string to be ISO8601-formatted."))
```

Dropping `.482` from the string decodes fine, so the fractional seconds are the trigger. The backend cannot easily stop emitting milliseconds. Does `.iso8601` map to a formatter with a fixed option set that excludes fractional seconds, and is a `.custom` strategy with two formatters (with and without) the usual fix, or is there a built-in that handles both?

title: catch (e: Exception) swallows CancellationException and the coroutine keeps running
NullPointerException from a Java getter even though the Kotlin type says non-null
content:
Kotlin 2.1 calling into a Java 21 library we do not own.

```
// Java
public class Config {
    public String getRegion() { return props.get("region"); } // can return null
}
```

```
// Kotlin
val region: String = config.region
println(region.uppercase())
```

```bash
java.lang.NullPointerException: config.getRegion() must not be null
	at com.example.Boot.start(Boot.kt:14)
```

The crash is on line 14 (the assignment), not at `uppercase()`, and the Kotlin compiler gave me no warning — IDE inspection shows the type as `String!`. If I declare `val region: String? = config.region` the null flows through fine. Where exactly is that null check being inserted, and is there a compiler flag or annotation on the Java side that would have made this a compile-time error instead?

title: Gradle: 'Inconsistent JVM-target compatibility' between compileJava 21 and compileKotlin 17
content: Kotlin 2.1 with the Gradle Kotlin plugin, Gradle 8.10, on a mixed Java/Kotlin module. The build fails with `Inconsistent JVM-target compatibility detected for tasks 'compileJava' (21) and 'compileKotlin' (17)`. My build script sets `java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }` but also has an older `kotlinOptions.jvmTarget = "17"` line that predates the toolchain block. I have seen three different suggested fixes — setting `compilerOptions.jvmTarget`, setting `kotlin { jvmToolchain(21) }`, and setting `sourceCompatibility`/`targetCompatibility` — and I do not know which of these are equivalent, which one wins if two are present, or whether the toolchain also decides which JDK actually runs the compiler daemon.

title: LateInitializationError: Field '_client' has not been initialized on the first request
type 'List<dynamic>' is not a subtype of type 'List<String>' after jsonDecode
content:
Dart 3.6. Decoding a JSON body and assigning a nested array fails at runtime, not at compile time.

```
final data = jsonDecode(body) as Map<String, dynamic>;
final List<String> tags = data['tags'];
```

```bash
type 'List<dynamic>' is not a subtype of type 'List<String>' in type cast
```

The payload really is `{"tags": ["a", "b"]}`, so every element is a string — but the static type of the list `jsonDecode` produces is `List<dynamic>`. `data['tags'] as List<String>` fails the same way, while `(data['tags'] as List).cast<String>()` works and so does `List<String>.from(data['tags'])`. Do `cast` and `from` differ in when they check the elements (lazily on access versus eagerly on construction), and which one should I prefer for data coming off the network?

title: Illegal argument in isolate message when passing a closure to Isolate.spawn
setState() called after dispose() when an await finishes after the user leaves the screen
content:
Flutter 3.27. Navigating away from a screen while a fetch is in flight throws in debug and logs a red screen in the console.

```
Future<void> _load() async {
  final data = await api.fetch();
  setState(() => _items = data);
}
```

```bash
Flutter Error: setState() called after dispose(): _FeedPageState#3a2f1
(lifecycle state: defunct, not mounted)
This error happens if you call setState() on a State object for a widget that
no longer appears in the widget tree.
```

Guarding with `if (!mounted) return;` before `setState` removes the error, and the analyzer even suggests it. But I still see the network request complete and its result thrown away, and in a couple of places I need the result (to write it to a cache). Is `mounted` the whole answer, or should the request be cancelled on `dispose` — and is there a standard way to cancel a `Future` that a plain `async` function returns?

title: Reordering a ListView with stateful children keeps the state on the wrong row
content:
Flutter 3.27. Each row is a `StatefulWidget` holding a small local count. When I remove the first item, the counts stay in place instead of moving with their rows.

```
ListView(
  children: _items
      .map((item) => CounterTile(label: item.label))
      .toList(),
)
```

With items A(count 3), B(0), C(0), removing A leaves B showing 3. I expected B to keep its own 0. Adding `key: ValueKey(item.id)` to `CounterTile` fixes it. I would like to understand what the framework matches on during reconciliation when no key is present, why the label updates correctly but the `State` does not follow, and whether `ObjectKey` or `UniqueKey` would be wrong choices here.

title: MissingPluginException for shared_preferences after a hot restart on Android
content: Flutter 3.27, Android. After adding `shared_preferences` and doing a hot restart, every call throws `MissingPluginException(No implementation found for method getAll on channel plugins.flutter.io/shared_preferences)`. A full stop and `flutter run` makes it work; the next hot restart brings it back. I have already run `flutter clean`, `flutter pub get`, and deleted `.dart_tool`. It reproduces on a physical device and an emulator, but not on iOS. My understanding is that plugin registration happens once when the engine attaches, and hot restart resets Dart state without re-running native registration — but I also call one preference read from a background isolate for a scheduled task, which I suspect never had a registrant at all. Which of these two is the actual cause, and how do I tell them apart from the log?
